prompt: Opponent: "Homework must stay, because students who do homework get better grades." Pick the strongest rebuttal.
context: Motion: This House would ban homework in primary school.

choices.text: That's correlation: diligent students both do homework and get good grades — the homework may add nothing.
choices.explanation: Correct — it attacks the causal inference at the heart of the argument, the load-bearing premise.

choices.text: Grades aren't everything.
choices.explanation: True but vague — it shifts ground without disputing their claim, and concedes their evidence.

choices.text: Some students dislike homework.
choices.explanation: Preference isn't a counter to an achievement claim; it's a different, weaker argument.

choices.text: Teachers assign too much homework anyway.
choices.explanation: A quantity complaint accepts homework's value and argues only about dosage — off-clash.

prompt: Opponent: "AI content labels will fix misinformation, because people will simply distrust what's labelled." Strongest rebuttal?
context: Motion: This House would require AI-generated content to carry a visible label.

choices.text: The danger inverts: unlabelled fakes gain a false stamp of authenticity, so partial enforcement makes deception more effective.
choices.explanation: Correct — a turn: their mechanism, incompletely enforced, produces the opposite of their promised impact.

choices.text: Labels are ugly.
choices.explanation: An aesthetic quibble that no judge weighs against a misinformation impact.

choices.text: Some people ignore labels.
choices.explanation: Mitigation only — it shrinks their impact but concedes the mechanism's direction.

choices.text: AI companies will complain.
choices.explanation: Stakeholder displeasure isn't an argument about whether the policy works.

prompt: "Banning single-use plastics will save the oceans." Which mechanism step is missing?

choices.text: How a national ban changes the (mostly non-domestic) sources of ocean plastic
choices.explanation: Correct — the chain from local ban to global ocean outcomes is asserted, not shown; most marine plastic enters via a few river systems.

choices.text: A definition of 'plastic'
choices.explanation: Reasonable definitions are assumed in ordinary debate; this isn't the gap a judge cares about.

choices.text: The name of the ocean being saved
choices.explanation: Specificity theatre — not a causal step.

choices.text: A celebrity endorsement
choices.explanation: Endorsements are not mechanisms.

prompt: "A four-day week will boost the economy because happier workers are more productive." What must still be proven?

choices.text: That the productivity gain is large enough to offset losing 20% of working hours
choices.explanation: Correct — the argument needs magnitude, not just direction. A real gain that's too small still sinks the case.

choices.text: That workers would enjoy a three-day weekend
choices.explanation: Safely assumed — and not where the case can fail.

choices.text: That economies exist
choices.explanation: Not in dispute.

choices.text: That some firms already tried it
choices.explanation: Trials support the claim but don't bridge the hours-versus-productivity arithmetic.

prompt: "My opponent isn't even old enough to vote, so you can ignore her case for lowering the voting age." Which fallacy?

choices.text: Ad hominem — attacking the speaker instead of the argument
choices.explanation: Correct — the speaker's age says nothing about whether her mechanism and evidence hold. If anything, she has relevant standing.

choices.text: Slippery slope
choices.explanation: No chain of escalating consequences was claimed.

choices.text: False dilemma
choices.explanation: No forced either/or choice appears here.

choices.text: Straw man
choices.explanation: The argument wasn't misrepresented — it was bypassed entirely for the person.

prompt: "Either we hold platforms fully liable for every post, or we accept a lawless internet. Since lawlessness is unacceptable, full liability it is." Which fallacy?

choices.text: False dilemma — intermediate liability regimes are excluded by assertion
choices.explanation: Correct — notice-and-takedown, amplification-only liability and safe-harbour conditions all exist between the two poles.

choices.text: Appeal to authority
choices.explanation: No authority was invoked.

choices.text: Circular reasoning
choices.explanation: The conclusion isn't smuggled into a premise; a premise (only two options) is simply false.

choices.text: Post hoc
choices.explanation: No temporal-causation confusion appears.

prompt: You argue school phone bans improve focus. Which single piece of evidence helps most?

choices.text: A multi-school study measuring test scores before and after bans, with comparison schools
choices.explanation: Correct — it measures the claimed outcome with a control group, directly supporting causation.

choices.text: A viral video of students on phones in class
choices.explanation: Vivid, but proves phones are used — not that banning them improves focus.

choices.text: Your own school experience
choices.explanation: An anecdote can illustrate a proven mechanism, but can't establish one.

choices.text: Total smartphone sales figures
choices.explanation: Measures market size, not classroom attention — impressive-sounding irrelevance.

prompt: Defending nuclear expansion on safety, your strongest statistic is:
context: Motion: This House would expand nuclear power as the core of the energy transition.

choices.text: Deaths per terawatt-hour across energy sources, where nuclear ranks among the safest
choices.explanation: Correct — it normalises risk per unit of energy, the honest comparison, and directly answers the safety objection.

choices.text: The count of reactors that have never had an accident
choices.explanation: Survivorship framing — it hides base rates and invites the obvious Chernobyl/Fukushima reply.

choices.text: Uranium's market price
choices.explanation: A cost datum aimed at a safety clash — wrong target.

choices.text: Public opinion polls on nuclear fear
choices.explanation: Measures perception of risk, which is precisely what you're arguing is miscalibrated.

prompt: Improve this: "Remote work is good. People like it. Also it saves money. And traffic is better. So it's good."

choices.text: Pick one claim, add its mechanism and a named impact: "Remote work returns the commute — over 200 hours a year — to workers, which is why retention rises where it's offered."
choices.explanation: Correct — one developed chain with a quantified impact beats four asserted fragments.

choices.text: Add three more benefits to the list
choices.explanation: More fragments deepen the core weakness: nothing is developed.

choices.text: Say 'it's good' with more conviction
choices.explanation: Confidence without mechanism is delivery polishing a hollow shell.

choices.text: Replace 'good' with 'excellent'
choices.explanation: A thesaurus is not an argument.

prompt: This opening buries its structure: "So, um, there are various considerations, and I'll touch on several themes that interconnect..." Fix it.

choices.text: "We win this round for two reasons: accountability and incentives. First, accountability..."
choices.explanation: Correct — a numbered preview gives the judge a map before the journey; every later sentence now has an address.

choices.text: "There are many nuanced perspectives worth exploring at length..."
choices.explanation: Restates the vagueness with better vocabulary.

choices.text: Skip the preview and dive into details
choices.explanation: Detail without a map is where judges get lost — and lost judges don't award content they couldn't track.

choices.text: "As I will explain later..." repeated throughout
choices.explanation: Promissory notes aren't structure; they defer it.

prompt: Opponent proposes UBI funded by "closing tax loopholes." Your most decisive cross-examination question?

choices.text: "What is your estimate of loophole revenue, and what fraction of the UBI bill does it cover?"
choices.explanation: Correct — it forces a numerical commitment their case must then survive; any answer helps you.

choices.text: "Don't you think UBI is lazy policy?"
choices.explanation: An insult with a question mark — invites a speech, commits them to nothing.

choices.text: "Have you personally read the tax code?"
choices.explanation: Ad hominem credentials-check; the judge learns nothing about the case.

choices.text: "Isn't funding complicated?"
choices.explanation: They'll agree and move on — no commitment extracted.

prompt: Opponent defends compulsory voting as "making democracy representative." Which question sets up your next speech best?

choices.text: "Is a ballot cast to avoid a fine an expression of political will, or of fine-avoidance?"
choices.explanation: Correct — either answer serves you: 'political will' is implausible; 'fine-avoidance' concedes the coerced-noise argument you're about to run.

choices.text: "Which countries have compulsory voting?"
choices.explanation: A facts quiz they can answer well — you've handed them a stage.

choices.text: "Why do you hate freedom?"
choices.explanation: Provocation reads as desperation and yields nothing usable.

choices.text: "Can you define democracy?"
choices.explanation: Definition-fishing without a trap planned; expect a competent answer and lost seconds.

prompt: You're For "ban junk-food sponsorship of sport." Which impact should headline your case?

choices.text: Reduced childhood exposure to health-halo marketing at population scale
choices.explanation: Correct — largest magnitude, clearest link to the policy, and hardest for the opposition to outweigh.

choices.text: Stadium aesthetics improve without garish logos
choices.explanation: Trivial magnitude; leading with it signals a weak case.

choices.text: Rival snack brands gain market share
choices.explanation: Distributional shuffle, not a social gain — and off-message for a health case.

choices.text: Sponsorship lawyers get more work
choices.explanation: A transition cost dressed as an impact.

prompt: Against "rotational Security Council membership," which impact do you lead with?

choices.text: Great powers abandoning the Council collapses the one forum that restrains them at all
choices.explanation: Correct — an irreversibility-plus-magnitude impact that frames reform as destroying the institution it claims to fix.

choices.text: Diplomats would need to relearn procedures
choices.explanation: Administrative friction — no judge weighs this against legitimacy claims.

choices.text: The UN building would need new nameplates
choices.explanation: Facetious; including it damages your credibility.

choices.text: Some current members would be annoyed
choices.explanation: Annoyance is not an impact unless you show what the annoyed do next — which is choice A, done properly.

prompt: In the algorithmic-feed debate, For argues user autonomy; Against argues ranked feeds filter harm. The central clash is:
context: Motion: This House would require social-media platforms to offer a non-algorithmic feed by default.

choices.text: Who should hold default power over attention — users by right, or platforms by competence?
choices.explanation: Correct — both cases are downstream of this question; the side that wins it wins the round.

choices.text: Whether algorithms exist
choices.explanation: Undisputed by both sides — no clash.

choices.text: Which platform has the best engineers
choices.explanation: Neither side's case depends on engineering league tables.

choices.text: Whether social media is enjoyable
choices.explanation: Adjacent mood, not the collision point of the two cases.

prompt: Artefact repatriation: For argues unjust acquisition voids title; Against argues universal museums maximise access and preservation. The clash?

choices.text: Whether historical justice or present-day utility should govern ownership
choices.explanation: Correct — every sub-argument (looting, loans, conservation, tourism) feeds this single collision.

choices.text: Whether museums should charge entry
choices.explanation: A pricing question orthogonal to ownership.

choices.text: Which country has better display cases
choices.explanation: A conservation detail both sides can solve; not decisive.

choices.text: Whether history is interesting
choices.explanation: Not in contention.

prompt: For "ban smartphones in schools," your teammate defines it as "all devices with screens, including laptops, forever." Repair it.

choices.text: "Personal phones stored during lesson hours, with medical and accessibility exemptions"
choices.explanation: Correct — defensible scope that preserves your mechanism while shedding the laptop-ban albatross the opposition would feast on.

choices.text: "Only phones we personally consider distracting"
choices.explanation: Subjective scope invites the 'who decides?' attack and looks evasive.

choices.text: Keep the broad definition and defend laptops too
choices.explanation: Voluntarily defending the weakest possible version of your own motion is strategic self-harm.

choices.text: "Phones, but only on Tuesdays"
choices.explanation: Arbitrary scope with no mechanism — parody of a definition.

prompt: Opponent defines "frequent flyer" as "anyone who flies at all" to make your progressive levy look like a total flight tax. Your repair?
context: Motion: This House would tax frequent flying at sharply progressive rates.

choices.text: "The levy starts at the second flight per year and escalates — the median flyer pays nothing, which is the entire design"
choices.explanation: Correct — re-anchors the definition in the motion's own wording ('progressive') and converts their straw man into your fairness argument.

choices.text: Accept their definition to avoid a definitions fight
choices.explanation: You'd spend the round defending a policy nobody proposed.

choices.text: "Definitions don't matter, let's talk values"
choices.explanation: Definitions decide what you must prove; waving them off cedes that decision.

choices.text: Refuse to engage until they apologise
choices.explanation: Theatrics; the judge just sees the straw man standing unanswered.

prompt: Closing For "pay students to finish school." The strongest final comparison:

choices.text: "Their world protects the principle that learning shouldn't be paid for; ours pays a small stipend and graduates thousands who'd otherwise drop out. Principles don't sign diplomas."
choices.explanation: Correct — two worlds, one concrete comparative, one repeatable line. This is what judges carry into deliberation.

choices.text: "We made strong arguments about incentives, evidence and fairness, as I'll now re-list"
choices.explanation: A table of contents, not a verdict.

choices.text: "Education is the future"
choices.explanation: A greeting-card line both sides could deliver — zero comparative work.

choices.text: "My opponent never understood the motion"
choices.explanation: Closing on an insult converts your final impression into pettiness.

prompt: Closing Against "platform liability for amplified content." Your best comparative close:

choices.text: "They promise accountability but deliver deletion: faced with ruinous liability, platforms won't judge speech — they'll remove it. Our world keeps both the internet and the lawsuits that matter; theirs keeps neither."
choices.explanation: Correct — it grants their goal, shows their mechanism betrays it, and lands a memorable both-worlds comparison.

choices.text: "Regulation is always bad"
choices.explanation: An ideological blanket that ignores the round's actual material.

choices.text: "As I said in my opening..." followed by the opening
choices.explanation: Verbatim recap surrenders the closing's unique job: comparison.

choices.text: "The internet is complicated, so vote Against"
choices.explanation: Complexity is a reason to think, not a reason to vote for you.
